summary: This script implements a blog search feature that answers questions about a blog by querying an AnythingLLM workspace (which handles vector search and LLM calls). It displays the AI-generated answer along with clickable source links, then runs a secondary exact-match search through the blog's frontmatter as a verification layer to catch relevant articles the semantic search might have missed.

explanations.9: This registers the command name and description in a lookup table so the parent script knows about this new 'blog-search' command.
explanations.14: This sets a default value for the blog directory location using parameter expansion — if AI_BLOG_DIR isn't already set, it defaults to ~/repositories/blog.
explanations.20: The -z test checks if the string is empty; the :- syntax provides a default value if the variable doesn't exist, so this line checks if the API key is missing.
explanations.26: This uses curl to ping the AnythingLLM server with a 2-second timeout — if it fails silently, the service is unreachable.
explanations.35: The -t 1 test checks if file descriptor 1 (stdout) is connected to a terminal, allowing the script to format output differently for interactive shells versus piped output.
explanations.36: This uses ANSI escape codes to create a hyperlink: the \e]8;; syntax is the OSC 8 protocol for terminal hyperlinks, while \e[1;32m makes the bullet bright green and \e[4m underlines the title.
explanations.37: The :t syntax removes the directory path from a URL, leaving only the filename.
explanations.44: The $* expands all arguments as a single string, so if you run 'ai-blog-search what is docker', question becomes 'what is docker'.
explanations.62: The RANDOM variable generates a random number; using it twice with $$ (process ID) creates a unique session ID so each question starts fresh instead of continuing previous conversations.
explanations.64: The @- tells curl to read the JSON from stdin (piped in from jq), treating it as binary data to avoid any encoding issues.
explanations.71: This extracts the error field from the JSON response, or returns nothing if no error exists; the // empty syntax is jq's way of providing a fallback value.
explanations.81: This extracts source documents from the response, filters to only those marked as links, reformats them, removes duplicates, and outputs them as tab-separated URL and title pairs.
explanations.90: The (f) flag in parameter expansion splits the string by newlines; this loop processes each source line separately.
explanations.91: These parameter expansions extract the URL (everything before the tab) and title (everything after the tab) from each line.
explanations.102: The noglob alias prevents zsh from interpreting ? and * in the question as file globbing patterns, which would otherwise cause 'no matches found' errors.
explanations.128: This chain of expansions: converts to lowercase (L), removes non-alphanumeric characters replacing with spaces (//[^[:alnum:]]/ ), splits on spaces (s: :), and removes duplicates (u).
explanations.134: This sets a ceiling threshold — articles matching a word more than 10% of the time are considered too common to be useful keywords.
explanations.143: This grep searches frontmatter fields (title, slug, description, mainTag, and tags) for the word, using -E for regex and -i for case-insensitive matching.
explanations.161: This extracts the slug field from frontmatter using sed: -n suppresses default output, the s command does substitution, head -1 takes the first match, and the final seds strip surrounding quotes.
